newsitem.title: USA: Duke Power poised to push into gas sector.
newsitem.headline: Duke Power poised to push into gas sector.

text.p: When Bill Grigg was tapped to lead Duke Power Co in January 1994, he understood his new role as chairman would be to prepare the utility for the era of competition.

That meant Grigg had to find ways to keep prices low and services high at Duke Power, an investor-owned electric utility that generates, transmits and sells electricity. Today, nearly three years after Grigg was named chairman (and as retirement looms) he has turned the company into a $4.68 billion enterprise set to enter the natural gas market.

"Gas is clearly the fuel of choice for new power generation going forward...which in effect means that it will control the price of electricity," Grigg said. "It makes makes sense for us to have control over that fuel supply."

Duke Power, the sixth-ranked U.S. investor-owned electric utility, is based here and operates throughout central North Carolina and the western portion of South Carolina. It operates outside of its service area through unit Duke Energy Group Inc and explores new technologies through Duke Engineering & Services, Inc.
"Its diversity has been in the energy area and that is a strength because they're playing off their expertise," said Oppenheimer & Co analyst Peter Hark.
Touted as one of the finest utilities in the country, Duke Power earned $714.5 million, or $3.25 a share, last year.

"Duke Power is perceived to be one of the best run electric utility companies in the nation. They have an extremely clean balance sheet," said Hark, noting that it has just 40 percent debt. And natural gas will soon be added to its landscape of three nuclear generating stations, eight coal-fired stations and 38 hydroelectric stations.
On Monday, Duke Power and Houston-based PanEnergy Corp announced their Boards of Directors agreed to merge in a deal that swaps PanEnergy shares for Duke Power shares worth about $7.7 billion.

The stock acquisition of PanEnergy, the No. 3 marketer of natural gas in North America, was due to be completed late next year provided there no regulatory snags and change the name it has held for 92 years to Duke Energy Corp.
A successful deal would stretch Duke's realm of influence along the East Coast as far noth as the New England states of Maine and Connecticut and as far south as Texas.
It would also reach into the Midwest where PanEnergy has markets.

"As we envision expanding the electric business nationally we need a platform on which to do that," said Duke Power President Richard Priory, who becomes chairman after Grigg retires late next year when the merger should be completed.

"Clearly, PanEnergy has a very extensive platform in 30 states and has gas positions in 48 states in North America. So that clearly leaves us with a platform to geographically expand our business and create a national presence in the delivery of energy," Priory continued.
Seeking to position itself for new revenues from a deregulated energy arena, Duke Power has long sought presence in the national and international electricity markets.

Though the company's existing joint venture, with wholesale and retail power seller Louis Dreyfus expanded business beyond its immediate service territory, deregulation was expected to have benefits beyond just selling power.
Deregulation opens markets and broadens competition. It would allow Duke Power to ship electricity directly to a competitor's customer. And with gas, Duke could meet all customer demands for energy.
Deregulated electricity and gas reportedly retails for more than $250 billion in the United States alone.

"In the energy services business customers are increasingly asking for energy solutions; not BTU solutions, not kilowatt solutions. To be able to provide that we think gives us a significant competitive advantage," Grigg said.
